title: Thessaloniki Awards: Jacqueline Lentzou’s ‘A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra’ Wins the Golden Alexander
full_text: × Nov 15, 2026 5:45am PT Thessaloniki Awards: Jacqueline Lentzou’s ‘A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra’ Wins the Golden Alexander The Greek filmmaker's sophomore feature earned her best director honors in the Venice Film Festival's Horizons strand. By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest Thessaloniki Awards: Jacqueline Lentzou’s ‘A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra’ Wins the Golden Alexander 2 hours ago Venice Prizewinner ‘A Day in the Life of Jo’ Explores ‘Who and What We Truly Are’ Through Emotional Journey of Ordinary, Remarkable Teenage Girl 1 day ago ‘Hold Onto Me’ Director Myrsini Aristidou Kicks Off Historic Oscar Campaign for Sundance Audience Award Winner: ‘I Really Feel Like We’re Underdogs’ 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra" (Courtesy of Thessaloniki Film Festival) Jacqueline Lentzou ’s “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra” won the top prize Sunday at the Thessaloniki Film Festival , taking home the Golden Alexander for best feature film in the Arrivals international competition section. The Greek filmmaker’s sophomore feature premiered in the Venice Film Festival’s Horizons strand, where it won the award for best director. It’s since gone on to play at the New York Film Festival, the BFI London Film Festival and the Busan Film Festival. Related Stories Apple Services Revenue Hits New Record of $31.6 Billion in September Quarter, but Growth Is Slowing Down Inspired by true events, “ A Day in the Life of Jo ” follows the unruly, melancholic 15-year-old Jo — played by newcomer Evia Andriopoulou — as she navigates the ups and downs of a typical day in a typical teenager’s life. Drifting through a series of seemingly unrelated and inconsequential events, that otherwise ordinary day is turned upside-down with the arrival of Phaedra (Anastasia Gouliamou), a bookish classmate whose warbling rendition of an old love ballad reduces Jo to tears. In an instant, her life — her drab, unremarkable day — becomes full of possibility, hurtling toward both tragedy and transformation. The film scooped a trio of awards on Sunday, as well as a Special Mention for Andriopoulou. The Silver Alexander for best director went to Pauline Julier and Nicolas Chapoulier for “ Les Indes ,” which had its premiere in the Venice Film Festival’s Venice Days strand. The writer-director duo’s feature debut is set in 1652 and follows three men as they transport a painting across a Europe ravaged by wars and uprisings. Best acting honors in the Arrivals competition went to Caique Copque and Italo Martins for “The Riverbank,” a queer erotic thriller from Brazilian directors Matheus Farias and Enock Carvalho that premiered in competition in Locarno. Best actress went to Arisa Sasaki, for Konstantina Kotzamani’s Cannes Un Certain Regard-premiering debut feature “Titanic Ocean,” an offbeat coming-of-age story set at a boarding school for aspiring mermaids in Japan. In the festival’s Meet the Neighbors+ competition section, which includes debut or sophomore films from the 36 countries of Southeastern Europe, the Mediterranean and the Middle East, the Golden Alexander for best feature went to “ Dua ,” by Kosovan filmmaker Blerta Basholli . Premiering in Cannes’ Critics’ Week strand, the director’s sophomore feature tells the story of a 13-year-old girl coming of age in the shadow of the Kosovo War. The section’s Silver Alexander for best director went to Abdallah Alkhatib for “ Chronicles From the Siege .” The winner of the Berlinale’s Perspectives award for debuts, the film presents vignettes of Palestinian lives in Gaza and in refugee camps. The award for best actor went to Alexis Manenti and Julian Świeżewski for “Flesh and Fuel,” French filmmaker Pierre Le Gall’s story about a passionate love affair between two long-distance truck drivers. Premiering in Cannes’ Critics Week, it took the top prize at the Zurich Film Festival and also earned Le Gall an award for best screenplay Sunday in Thessaloniki. Maria Petrova, the young star of Cypriot filmmaker Myrsini Aristidou’s Sundance Audience Prize-winning “ Hold Onto Me ,” took home the award for best actress. In the Film Forward competition section showcasing innovative filmmaking, the Golden Alexander went to Hoda Taheri and Boris Hadžija’s “I Plant My Hand in the Garden,” while the Silver Alexander went to Rob Rice for “Ponderosa,” whose star Alexis Blendel won the prize for best actress. The award for Best Artistic Achievement went to Argyris Germanidis’ “Particles of Dust,” while best actor honors went to Alexis Kalofolias for “Under the Judas Tree.” Here’s a rundown of the winners in the Thessaloniki Film Festival’s three competition sections: Arrivals Golden Alexander : “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra,” Jacqueline Lentzou Silver Alexander : Pauline Julier and Nicolas Chapoulier, “Les Indes” Best actor : Caique Copque and Italo Martins, “The Riverbank” Best actress : Arisa Sasaki, “Titanic Ocean” Special Mention : Evita Andriopoulou, “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra” Meet the Neighbors+ Golden Alexander : “Dua,” Blerta Basholli Silver Alexander : Abdallah Alkhatib, “Chronicles From the Siege” Best actor : Alexis Manenti and Julian Świeżewski, “Flesh and Fuel” Best actress : Maria Petrova, “Hold Onto Me” Best screenplay : “Flesh and Fuel,” Pierre Le Gall Film Forward Golden Alexander : “I Plant My Hand in the Garden,” Hoda Taheri and Boris Hadžija Silver Alexander : Rob Rice, “Ponderosa” Best artistic achievement : “Particles of Dust,” Argyris Germanidis Best actress : Alexis Blendel, “Ponderosa” Best actor : Alexis Kalofolias, “Under the Judas Tree” Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Bumps ‘Choosin’ Texas’ Out of No. 1 on Hot 100; ‘Encore’ Tracks Fill Four Out of Five Top Slots Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as ‘Life of a Showgirl’ Stays on Top in Week 2 of ‘Encore’ Rebound Taylor Swift Premieres ‘Patient Zero’ Music Video at VMAs, Turning Her New ‘Showgirl: Encore’ Single Into a Dramatic Ghost Story Bill Maher Fires Back at Trump by Comparing Him to Taylor Swift Todd Rundgren Slams Taylor Swift, Says She ‘Ruined Music’ and Is ‘the Apotheosis of Mediocrity’ Dakota Johnson on Being in Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Music Video: ‘We Respect Each Other’s Creative Minds’ Loading comments...

title: Seville European Film Festival Prizes: ‘You Don’t Belong Here,’ ‘Falling House,’ ’Adult Supervision’ Win Big
full_text: × Nov 15, 2026 4:52am PT Seville European Film Festival Prizes: ‘You Don’t Belong Here,’ ‘Falling House,’ ’Adult Supervision’ Win Big Italy’s ‘Children of the Monkey,’ Spain’s ‘El Director’ and ‘Wild Is the Wind’ also score top prizes By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Seville European Film Festival Prizes: ‘You Don’t Belong Here,’ ‘Falling House,’ ’Adult Supervision’ Win Big 3 hours ago Huelva Ibero-American Film Festival: Genre Mashups, a Vibrant Brazil and an Award for the One-Off Paulina García 2 days ago 10 Huelva Festival Standouts From ‘La Bola Negra’ to a Vibrant ‘Funk’ Musical and the Latest from ‘Dive’ Director Lucía Puenzo 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'You Don't Belong Here' Courtesy of the Seville European Film Festival Romania’s Florin Şerban added a Seville Golden Giraldillo to a Golden Leopard at Locarno on Saturday, winning Best Film in main competition at the 2026 Seville European Film Festival which also prized Venice New Horizons buzz title “Falling House” and Sweden’s Oscar entry “Adult Supervision.” Seville’s biggest world premiere, Spain’s “The Director,” also scored a high profile award at a festival which works at multiple levels: a new talent springboard, an industry hub, further recognition for the large number ofEuropean films which partly fly under the radar, and a springboard for European productions breaking out to international sales or consolidating their contention for Oscar International Feature Film shortlist recognition. Related Stories Apple Services Revenue Hits New Record of $31.6 Billion in September Quarter, but Growth Is Slowing Down Notably, victors at Seville’s Saturday’s prize announcement also took in Marcus Schleinzer ’s Austrian Oscar entry “Rose” and Abinash Bikram Shah ’s “Elephants in the Fog,” a submission from Nepal. A closer look at Seville main competition winners: “You Don’t Belong Here,” (Florin Şerban) Described by Variety as “a somber study of anti-Roma racism in the country, “You Don’t Belong Here” marks the fourth feature from Şerban whose 2010 debut, “If I Want to Whistle, I Whistle,” took a Berlinale Grand Prix. Shot in hallmark drab Romanian cinema tones, which won Bogdan Ionescu Best Artistic Direction, “You Don’t Belong Here” turns on a respected, upright surgeon who discovers his son has helped beat to death a Roma man. Filmed in static shoots with pauses between dialog, the film won four awards at Locarno, including but, as Variety noted at Locarno, failed to impress Variety critic Jay Weissberg who lamented that the film “opens with great promise and finishes with a stupefyingly misguided coda.” “Falling House,” ( Mohsen Gharaei ) Another tale of threatened patriarchy, Iranian filmmaker Mohsen Gharaei’s “Falling House” scored Seville’s Grand Jury Prize, plus a nod for Best Editing for Evelyn Rack and Emad Khodabakhsh. Bowing in Venice Horizons, and described by the director as a story about “lost freedom,” it turns on a prison guard who, learning his eldest daughter plans to escape to Turkey for a career in modelling, incarcerates his own family in a house facing demolition. Sold by Paradise City Sales. “Falling House” has closed a first batch of deals with France’s Jokers Films for France, Italy’s Wanted Cinema and Karma Films for Spain. “Adult Supervision,” ( Alex Schulman ) Much of Seville’s focus is on new or emerging talent. Of all its feature debuts, the biggest winner was “Adult Supervision,” from well-known Swedish author and podcast host Alex Schulman which has has sold widely by Heretic, including to WBD, Place and Vertigo. The film’s double wins – a Puerta América Award and Best Actor prize – will stoke more word around Sweden’s International Feature Oscar entry, which was another buzz title which has struck promising first sales, selling widely for Heretic, including to WBD, Place and Vertigo. “El Director,” ( Dani de la Orden , Spain) Seville’s biggest new push at Frame, its industry umbrella, saw it partner with Spain’s ICAA film agency to launch Insula, a screenplay market featuring 58 titles. Its jury president this year was AMPAS VP Howard A. Rodman, a screenwriter best known for “Savage Grace” and “August,” So Best Screenplay was a key plaudit, which went to a film where words are crucial: Dani de la Orden’s “El Director,” based on David Jiménez’s lid-lifting autobiographical non-fiction book about his time as editor-in-chief at newspaper El Mundo, and his battle to protect riotous journalism against the vested economic and political interests to often served. The prize went more specifically to two institutions on Spain’s film-TV scene: Alejandro Hernández, a co-writer on films and series by Alejandro Amenábar (“The Captive”) and Mariano Barroso (“The Farad”) and Michel Gaztambide, who broke out co-writing Julio Medem’s debut “Cows,” back in 1992, before penning many of the films and series by Enrique Urbizu plus Victor Erice’s 2023 “Close Your Eyes.” “Children of the Monkey,” (Tomasso Landucci) The Seville European Film Festival also highlights movies which merit more recognition. One case in point: Tomasso Landucci’s Venice Horizons Best Screenplay and Best Actor (Riccardo Scamarcio) winner “Children of the Monkey,” which this time round at Seville scored Best Director. In its portrayal of the dilemma of the father of a disabled son, “Children of the Monkey” is both deeply felt and impressively sensitive in the way it explores his painful emotional predicament,”Diego Lerer, one of the critics who did catch the film in Venice, wrote in his blog Micropsia. “Wild Is the Wind,” (“Tralovento,” Eloy Domínguez Serén) A second prize for Spain: Galician actress Melania Cruz (“Gangs of Galicia”) won her biggest prize to date, scooping best actress for her lead turn in “Wild With the Wind.” the feature debut of Eloy Domínguez Serén, from a screenplay co-written with top Catalan auteur Meritxell Colell (“Far From the Trees”). Cruz plays Ana, who returns to her home village in rural Galicia after her father’s death, but stays to oppose a utility company’s plans to build a wind farm on community land. Bowing at Mexico’s Morelia Festival, the film won praise, such as in aCriticalia.com review, for its measured pace. Cruz’s performance and nuanced view of the wind farm project. title: Russell Brand Accuser Waives Anonymity, Alleging She Was Raped By Star At Age Of 16
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Russell Brand Accuser Waives Anonymity, Alleging She Was Raped By Star At Age Of 16 HBO Releases Surprise ‘Harry Potter’ Clip Of Hogwarts Banquet ‘Dept. Q’ Crew Member Dies On Set After Season 2 Wrapped Filming In Edinburgh View All November 15, 2026 4:09am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mia Latter accuses Russell Brand of rape Getty One of Russell Brand ‘s accusers has waived her legal right to anonymity after the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star was imprisoned for rape and sexual assault. In an interview with The Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin (watch below), Mia Latter alleged that she was orally raped by Brand in 2006, when she was aged 16 and he was 30. She alleged that Brand referred to her as “the child” during their relationship, which she now considers to have been emotionally and sexually abusive. Latter was one of the four women who spoke to The Times , Sunday Times , and Channel 4 in 2023. Their testimony inspired other women to make criminal complaints against Brand, ultimately leading to his conviction at London’s Southwark Crown Court earlier this month. Related Stories News Russell Brand Accused Of Sexual Misconduct By Six More Women After Rape Conviction News BBC Boss Challenged By Staff Over Culture Of "Reverence" Towards Powerful Stars Brand has consistently denied wrongdoing. When Latter’s allegations were first published in 2023, Brand denied the claims and said it was part of a campaign by the “mainstream media” to silence him. Watch on Deadline Latter, now 37, has gone public because she is campaigning for a change in UK law, calling for the introduction of a “staggered” age of consent, mirroring some U.S. states, including Florida. This would outlaw relationships between 16 year olds and adults, but would protect relationships between teenagers who are above the age of consent. Latter, who was known as Alice in earlier reporting, first met Brand in central London when she was out shopping. Brand, who was hosting MTV shows at the time, approached her in the street and asked for her number. They exchanged texts, met for a date, and ended up back at his apartment. Latter alleged that Brand attempted to give her oral sex, even though she was “squirming” in her seat. Latter alleged that Brand requested that she keep their three-month relationship secret, though her parents were “distraught” by their association. Brand encouraged Latter to skip school, sending cars to pick her up. Russell Brand Getty Towards the end of their relationship, Latter alleged that Brand orally raped her. “He ended up forcing me against the headboard [of the bed] and I couldn’t move, and he orally raped me — and I was choking and crying,” she told The Sunday Times. “I was trying to push him off, so he knew that I didn’t want him to be doing that, and so then I ended up having to hit him in the stomach to get him off. I’ve never hit anyone [before] and … he said: ‘I just wanted to see your mascara run.’” Brand discussed his relationship with Latter during an appearance on The Megyn Kelly Show in April . He admitted that his relationship with Latter had been “exploitative” and that he had “manipulated” consent. During the same interview, he described his behavior with women as “awful but lawful.” Latter said: “If [consent is] manipulated, it’s not given. That’s not how that works. I think also [in] doing that interview, he was quite successful in distracting people … by saying, ‘It was immoral, it wasn’t illegal.’ Well, actually something illegal happened within that relationship.” Latter was interviewed by the police in 2024, but said she was told by the Crown Prosecution Service that she would not be included in the trial, partly because of Brand’s appearance on Megyn Kelly’s show. “I was devastated by it,” she told The Sunday Times. Latter also expressed dismay at the media organizations and people who stood by Brand. “At times, I felt angrier with these media organizations than I have with him, because he’s a monstrous person, but to be that spineless,” she said. “He couldn’t have done this for so long without these people enabling it, and disregarding the women who made complaints at the time.” On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. The Sun newspaper reported on Sunday that Brand has been moved to Littlehey Prison, a jail for men who have been convicted of sexual offenses. title: ‘Woman Unknown’ Breakout Mathilde Arcel on Her Venice Award-Winning Performance and Life After Her Lido Triumph: ‘Everything Is Open’
full_text: × Nov 15, 2026 3:17am PT ‘Woman Unknown’ Breakout Mathilde Arcel on Her Venice Award-Winning Performance and Life After Her Lido Triumph: ‘Everything Is Open’ The 30-year-old has also been nominated for best actress at the European Film Awards, while May el-Toukhy's Golden Lion winner is representing Denmark in the best international feature race at the Oscars By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest Thessaloniki Awards: Jacqueline Lentzou’s ‘A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra’ Wins the Golden Alexander 2 hours ago Venice Prizewinner ‘A Day in the Life of Jo’ Explores ‘Who and What We Truly Are’ Through Emotional Journey of Ordinary, Remarkable Teenage Girl 1 day ago ‘Hold Onto Me’ Director Myrsini Aristidou Kicks Off Historic Oscar Campaign for Sundance Audience Award Winner: ‘I Really Feel Like We’re Underdogs’ 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Jasper Spanning Danish actress Mathilde Arcel would be the first to admit she didn’t see this coming. It’s been hardly two months since Arcel, in her first-ever leading role in a feature film, was awarded the Volpi Cup for best actress for her breakout performance in “Woman Unknown,” May el-Toukhy ’s riveting, post-World War II drama that was also feted with the festival’s Golden Lion . Praised by Variety ‘s Beatrice Loayza for her “magnetic” performance, Arcel plays a young housemaid whose intimate relationship with a German soldier during World War II threatens her future. Related Stories Apple Services Revenue Hits New Record of $31.6 Billion in September Quarter, but Growth Is Slowing Down Now, on the eve of the closing ceremony of the Thessaloniki Film Festival , which wraps Nov. 15 with el-Toukhy’s Venice winner, Arcel is taking in the news that she’s among the six nominees for best actress at the European Film Awards, whose nominations were announced Saturday afternoon in Thessaloniki. For Arcel, whose grandmother comes from the Greek island of Lesvos, the award ceremony, which will be held in Athens in January, feels like “a weird kind of homecoming.” “I feel so lucky,” she says. Over coffee at Thessaloniki’s Mediterranean Palace, the 30-year-old still seems awestruck by her meteoric rise. Just over two months ago, Arcel was herself a relative unknown, with a career that had mostly spanned the stage and television. Before her Venice breakout, her only appearances on the big screen were in supporting roles. After accepting best actress honors on the Lido, Arcel revealed to Danish media that she’d been collecting unemployment benefits ahead of the Italian fest; she was on her way to report to a job center in Copenhagen when she got word that she needed to fly back to Venice for the award ceremony. Reflecting in Thessaloniki on what she describes with wide eyes as “an adventure,” Arcel says, laughing, “It’s only downhill from here, right?” “Woman Unknown” draws on accounts of the many women across Europe who in peacetime were publicly shamed for their actions during the Nazi occupation — women whose stories have been swept to the margins of the collective memory of World War II. Accepting the Golden Lion in Venice, el-Touky acknowledged that the film had been “incredibly challenging to make financially, logistically, emotionally,” adding that “what kept me going was the urgent need to illuminate the unknown women of our common history, to make them known.” For Arcel, that history hit close to home. “I remember my Danish grandma, when I asked about the war, she told me that she was a kid on the day of the liberation, and she remembered that all of these women, her neighbors, were suddenly being pulled out onto the street. Other neighbors spitting at them, calling them names. Their hair was cut off,” Arcel says. “It really stuck with me, that this was…her most vivid memory from the occupation.” Still, until she began researching the part, the actress says she “didn’t know how vast this phenomenon was, all across Europe, how these women were treated.” Mathilde Arcel won the Volpi Cup for best actress at the Venice Film Festival . ‘Woman Unknown’ Courtesy of Seminci In some ways, Arcel might have been destined for the part; after graduating from drama school in Copenhagen, she says, el-Toukhy was “the first person I wrote to.” “I wrote to her that I really loved her movies and I would love to work with her. I didn’t think it would happen,” she says. “But then she called me in for a casting. I definitely didn’t think I would get it, because I felt like the role had a different vibe to it than what I thought at that time was a natural fit for me…. It was very different from the parts I’d played. It was a new kind of challenge.” Her feelings changed once she unexpectedly landed the role, and she began to discuss the part with el-Toukhy. “When I read it, I couldn’t get a read on [the character of Marie] immediately,” she says. “It was kind of like detective work when I started working with her to see what kind of person she is and why she does what she does. It was intriguing.” As with the director’s 2019 drama “Queen of Hearts,” which stars Trine Dyrholm as a successful lawyer whose life gets turned upside down by an illicit affair, Arcel praises el-Toukhy for her ability to craft female characters “that are complex in their morality,” something that she describes as “quite rare.” Working with the Danish Egyptian filmmaker was a “very collaborative process,” she adds, describing the duo as “a good team.” “I wanted to know as much as I could about the period. What kind of dreams did they have at that time? What kind of movies did they watch? What kind of music did they hear?” Arcel says. “May is also very hands-on in the research. We both want to do everything we can to know as much as possible.” Next up for Arcel is a trip to the Marrakech Film Festival, where “Woman Unknown” plays in the festival’s Horizons section, while an Oscar campaign in the best international feature category is also underway, after Denmark selected the film as its submission for the 99th Academy Awards. Scripts have begun pouring in and the actress — who now has U.S. representation — has cleared her calendar for the next six months as she considers various offers. For now, it’s too soon to say what comes next. “It’s very different, very exciting,” she says. “It feels like being on the verge of something that might happen and might not even happen. A lot of dreams and hopes. Everything is open.” The Thessaloniki Film Festival runs Nov. 5 – 15. Bandung’s screenings are taking place at CGV Paris Van Java, while Malang’s are at Cinépolis Malang Town Square, with both editions running through Nov. 21. The move takes the festival to audiences who have tracked the Jakarta event from elsewhere in the country. Related Stories Apple Services Revenue Hits New Record of $31.6 Billion in September Quarter, but Growth Is Slowing Down The Bandung edition is programming 203 international titles drawn from 69 countries. Cristian Mungiu’s “ Fjord ,” which won this year’s Palme d’Or at Cannes, opened proceedings. Also on the slate are Beth de Araujo’s “Josephine,” which took both the Grand Jury Prize and the Audience Award in Sundance’s U.S. Dramatic Competition in 2026, and Marine Atlan’s “La Gradiva,” winner of the AMI Paris Grand Prize at this year’s Cannes Critics’ Week. Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime,” which picked up the Un Certain Regard Prize at Cannes, screens alongside Kurosawa Kiyoshi’s new feature “The Samurai and the Prisoner,” a Cannes Premiere selection. The festival’s online program, available until Nov. 21, includes Ildiko Enyedi’s “Silent Friend,” a Fipresci Prize winner at Venice in 2025, and Ilker Çatak’s “Yellow Letters,” this year’s Golden Bear winner at the Berlinale. Bandung Mayor Muhammad Farhan attended the opening night at CGV Paris Van Java. “Bandung World Cinema gives the local audience an unprecedented opportunity to watch alternative cinema outside of the mainstream Hollywood films that dominate the theaters. The hope is that this festival will foster a greater local appreciation for film, become a source of inspiration for cinephiles, and encourage aspiring filmmakers to pursue their dreams,” Farhan said. Frederica, executive director of Bandung World Cinema, said organizers had noticed keen interest from cinephiles beyond Jakarta for years. “Bringing the Jakarta World Cinema experience to Bandung and Malang for the first time has been a long time coming,” she said. “Over the next eight days, audiences in both cities will experience the exact same caliber of bold, thought-provoking, and celebrated global cinema that defines JWC.” Unlike the Jakarta event, Bandung will wrap on Nov. 21 with a free open-air screening for the general public. The outdoor program will feature work by students at Bandung universities and winners of the KlikFilm Short Movie Competition, before closing with a restored version of “Lewat Djam Malam” (“After the Curfew”), Usmar Ismail’s 1954 Indonesian classic. title: Listen to the River! ‘Arrow for a Stone Heart’ Is a Poetic Hybrid Experience Told Through an Indigenous Lens
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 14, 2026 10:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source ‘Arrow for a Stone Heart’ Courtesy of PÖFF A pig-like creature is walking around in the territory of the indigenous Guaraní on the outskirts of São Paulo, Brazil. “My name is Rete, I am a peccary,” it tells us. And it shares what started happening to nature back in the days when the colonizers began to settle. “One day, those who are many started arriving.” Over time, the stones they brought started swallowing up more and more space, restricting an ancient river, plants and many creatures. Also in the indigenous territory, a woman named Jera Rete dreams. In her nightmares, the city invades her village. But there is also an old woman who keeps talking to her. And even the river has a voice – if you are only willing to listen. Related Stories Movies 'Fatherland' Wins Top Camerimage Prize as 'Wild Horse Nine' Nabs Audience Award Lifestyle L.A.'s Most Celebrated French Chef Is Staging a Comeback In her poetic debut feature, Arrow for a Stone Heart ( Flecha para Um Coração de Pedra ), writer, director and cinematographer Luiza Calagian, in collaboration with the local Guaraní indigenous community, transport us into the heart of the forest near the city. And the documentary-fiction hybrid’s narrative is very different for a reason. The way the indigenous people experience and narrate reality is different. From their perspective, myths, dreams, and relationships with non-humans connect different temporalities and perspectives. ‘Arrow for a Stone Heart’ Courtesy of PÖFF The cinematic, maybe even hallucinatory, journey that the movie takes us on elucidates the history of the community’s struggle. Cinema emerges as an opportunity for understanding and, possibly, change. Arrow for a Stone Heart celebrates its world premiere on Tuesday, Nov. 17, in the Rebels with a Cause Competition of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ) in Estonia. ‘Arrow for a Stone Heart’ Courtesy of PÖFF Calagian co-wrote the film with Jera Rete. Calagian also handled cinematography and shared the editing duties with Caio De. The producers are Vinicius Toro and Sabrina Zimmermann, with Bruno Cucio serving as executive producer. Utopia Docs is handling distribution and world sales. Ahead of the world premiere, Calagian told THR about how the idea for Arrow for a Stone Heart came about and its unique voice, look and feel. “I kind of grew up with this film. It’s been seven years now,” the creative explains. “The film began to transform as well, and at a certain point, I understood that it wouldn’t make sense for me to try to tell the story, which is the story of the Guaraní. It had to be told from their point of view and from their perspective rather than one that comes from the West.” So, how do you do that in a comprehensive way? “The mission became how do we bring the Guaraní cosmology, the Guaraní philosophy, the way that they see, organize, narrate and symbolize reality into the structure of a film, which is by its nature a Western thing,” Calagian tells THR . “But this also opened up the possibilities of transformation that this art has.” The first thing she started looking at was dreams. “The Guaraní are very, very, very connected to their dreams,” she explains. “They don’t understand dreams just as something that your mind creates or something that your imagination creates, but the dream for them is a form of connecting to other dimensions, other beings, other spirits, to people who are not here anymore, and to gods.” ‘Arrow for a Stone Heart’ Courtesy of PÖFF In the process, Jera became a close friend. “She embraced the project to the point that she became a co-writer,” Calagian shares with THR . “She also started organizing who was going to be in the film. The main characters other than her are her two daughters. One of the girls, her youngest, plays the river, and the older daughter, who also appears briefly at the end of the film, voiced Rete, the peccary. So everything kind of revolves around Jera. She is the leader of this village, and she became not only the co-writer but also the whole heart of the film.” The filmmaker also fell in love with Rete, the peccary. And the peccary became the symbol of her production company, Mata Fechada Filmes. “For me, it is a symbol,” Calagian says. “It has a lot to do with the magic of cinema. The Guaraní say it has the capacity of moving and traveling between worlds and entering different dimensions, different perspectives and visiting the gods.” Humans destroying the natural balance and colonization are recurring themes of Arrow for a Stone Heart . The river, for example, is considered one of the wisest and most powerful spirits for the Guaraní. “Even before colonization, when everything was more in harmony, the Guaraní were very careful and very respectful of those river spirits because they can be dangerous – they are not to be messed with,” the filmmaker highlights. “That’s why I wanted to include this character, the river, to tell her side of the story. Despite all of this destruction, there is still life in the river, which is amazing. Somehow, nature finds a way to survive, even in such adverse conditions. She represents an anthropomorphic presence.” Even words and language were chosen with care to properly represent the indigenous people’s view of the world. “Those who are many” is one of the recurring phrases, for example. “That is the common way they call the people who invaded,” Calagian tells THR . Luiza Calagian She has actually worked with the Guaraní for more than 10 years now, having in the past also focused on communications efforts to make their voice heard. “We were working on a campaign to make the government recognize the indigenous lands that they had inside the city, one of the biggest metropolises in the world,” the filmmaker notes. “There is a big historical dispute around the history of colonization, especially in São Paulo. There is a regional culture that celebrates the colonizers who were responsible for invading this territory, which has always been Guaraní territory.” That’s also where the film title, Arrow for a Stone Heart , comes from. It is not only a play on the phrase “heart of stone” for cruel or cold-hearted people but also a reference to the statues and other reminders and colonialism. “There are still a lot of historical monuments, a lot of street names, a lot of public political symbols that celebrate the colonizers, the people who killed and enslaved the indigenous people,” highlights Calagian. “We understood how important this dispute between narratives was, and that’s how this project was born.” Watch the trailer for Arrow for a Stone Heart here. title: Bowen Yang Makes Surprise ‘SNL’ Appearance as Jensen Huang as John Mulaney Pokes at FAA Ground Stop and Microsoft Outage in Cold Open
full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All November 14, 2026 8:57pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Screenshot Logo text Bowen Yang made a surprise appearance on Saturday Night Live to portray former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to warn a group of tech billionaires about how to decipher between “a woman who would actually want to have sex with you and a woman who is clearly a spy.” John Mulaney , who served as the host of the episode, kicked off the cold open by welcoming the group of moguls, including Sam Altman (Ben Marshall), Peter Thiel (James Austin Johnson), Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane), Mark Zuckerberg (Andrew Dismukes) and Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline). Related Stories TV Shane Gillis Addresses 'SNL' Monologue Backlash, Says He Promised the Show There Would Be "No Controversy" TV TV Ratings: 'SNL' Hits Two-Year High With Druski as Host “We are here to discuss an extremely sensitive matter of national security,” Mulaney began. “America needs you to learn the difference between a woman who would actually want to have sex with you and a woman who is clearly a spy,” he said. “Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned this week after he was caught having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.” “What do you think the lesson is here?” he asked, to which Wickline’s Amodei responded, “Never date a Chinese woman.” Dismukes’ Zuckerberg offered, “Never date a human woman.” “Never date anyone unless they become the Anti-Christ,” Johnson’s Thiel said. Mulaney joked that he needed to “chill with the Anti-Christ stuff,” which prompted him to respond, “Show us some respect. We do a lot for this country. Name one time technology has let us down.” The comedian then pointed to current events: “Yesterday, when every plane in America was grounded.” Thiel asked for “one more” example, which Mulaney affirmed, “The day before that when Microsoft Outlook went dark!” He then showed the tech billionaires a few venn diagrams to try and spell things out for the men, making way for Yang’s surprise return. “You know what, maybe what would help is if I hand it over to someone who learned this lesson the hard way,” Mulaney said, as the former SNL star then entered the scene. “It’s me! Jensen ‘hide your wife’ Huang!” Yang said. “When you invite Jensen over, you know it’s about to go down.” He joked, “Fellas, don’t be like me. Remember, women don’t like guys like us. That’s how we became guys like us.” Yang exited the SNL cast last December, with Saturday’s cameo marking his first appearance on the show since he left. He departed the series mid-season 51 with a heartfelt farewell sketch alongside Ariana Grande. Later in the Dec. 14 episode, Yang also appeared in a sketch as Mary Todd Lincoln, the role he began performing on Broadway this September in Oh, Mary! He sang a spoof of “And I Am Telling You I’m Not Going,” which prompted Mulaney to joke, “Wow! Now that’ll turn Abraham straight again.” the nation’s most prominent tech billionaires gather over an issue of national security pic.twitter.com/IRnpToBRGo — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) November 15, 2026 It was also announced in the episode that Amanda Seyfried will host the Dec. 5 episode of SNL , with Don Toliver as musical guest. During Mulaney’s monologue, he did a light Robert F. Kennedy Jr. impression, which merely turned out to be more of a criticism of the United States Secretary of Health and Human Services. He started by explaining that as a father, he often is around a lot of toddlers. “Whenever I’m with my son’s 4-year-old, 5-year-old friends, whenever I’m with a group of toddlers at art camp, preschool play dates, there’s always at least one little kid who for some reason, has a very scratchy or hoarse voice.” “Whenever a few are at my house, there’s always one like, ‘Do you have water balloons?’ Like, ‘Do you live alone?'” Mulaney said, continuing to repeat questions that his children’s friends ask him, using a raspy voice while saying, “I’m the U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services. My father was a good man, and I’m a lousy man, but I have same name. Am I good if I have same name as father?” Mulaney continued his impression, “No, please, let me be in charge of your bone and your tummy. Please allow me to control how your blood feels in your butt and everywhere. Stop the science! Robitussin taken during menstruation will cause telekinesis. This is clear from the pamphlets in my rental car.’” He then returned to his own voice, continuing to criticize RFK Jr. “I have right-wing friends that used to be down with him, no one likes him. You dumbass: Your thing can’t be the measles.” John Mulaney's monologue! pic.twitter.com/fZGfls92NE — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) November 15, 2026 Mulaney previously served as an SNL writer from 2008-2012. Although he was never a castmember, he has since returned to the show multiple times since his departure, making a plethora of cameos and hosting seven times. The comedian was joined by Phoebe Bridgers as musical guest, marking her second solo appearance (she’s also been on SNL as part of the musical group Boygenius). So far on season 52 , Jalen Brunson , Dakota Johnson , Shane Gillis , Inde Navarrette and Druski have each hosted. THR

title: Brandi Carlile’s All-Requests Tour Isn’t Just a Magnificent Stunt, but an Unusually Moving Transaction Between Performer and Audience: Concert Review
full_text: × Nov 14, 2026 7:24pm PT Brandi Carlile’s All-Requests Tour Isn’t Just a Magnificent Stunt, but an Unusually Moving Transaction Between Performer and Audience: Concert Review By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Brandi Carlile’s All-Requests Tour Isn’t Just a Magnificent Stunt, but an Unusually Moving Transaction Between Performer and Audience: Concert Review 12 hours ago Journey Announces Drummer Deen Castronovo Is Exiting Band, Days After Another Health Scare Forced His Second Mid-Show Departure 21 hours ago U2 Gets On Its Boots for First All-New Full-Length Record in Nine Years, ‘Carnaval de Luz,’ With More Callbacks to Band’s ’90s Peaks Than ’80s Glories: Album Review 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jen Horton Is it possible to plan for magic, serendipity, peak-level proficiency and finally sublimity by… really not planning at all? That is the question. On Brandi Carlile ‘s current “Burn the Setlist!” tour, the answer is clear: Sometimes Shangri-La really is best reached with a lost roadmap. The shortish 19-date outing Carlile is undertaking at the moment is the first all-requests tour in memory by any artist significant enough to have it show up on our radar. It might even be a historic first, as far as a proven headliner opting to play nothing but spontaneously generated live audience picks. Which is odd when you think about it, because doesn’t anyone who’s been to a lot of shows over the years have a favorite moment when a star got loose and succumbed to someone shouting out a favorite (though they usually don’t want to encourage that kind of behavior?). But at the opposite end of the scale from bar bands and tip jars, doing solely requests sounds like as much of a nightmare to most performers as it does a dream to hardcore fans. There are perfectly good reasons not to throw the song selections completely open to stans for roughly 2 hours and 40 minutes — as Carlile and her two bandmates, Phil and Tim Hanseroth , are doing now — when you have a recorded catalog of close to a hundred original songs, plus a repertoire of proven live cover choices. Who among even the greats of music has anything close to 100% recall? When the recent and distant pasts are both being dredged up, a good corollary to “Never let ’em see you sweat” might be: Never let ’em see you forget. Fortunately, Brandi Carlile and the Hanseroth twins are freaking elephants. Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre Jen Horton But making a point out of not planning is different from not being prepared. And Carlile and the brothers are prepared for this, first of all, by having brain chemistry that is clearly a little bit different from mine or probably yours, with the power not just to generate constant creative sparks but to put those sparks in an easily accessible lockbox. You’re either genetically predisposed to that kind of recall or you’re not, and at least a little part of why Carlile and the Hanseroths have been ideal partners since the turn of the millennium is that shared gift. Not that they came into the “Burn the Setlist!” tour relying completely on muscle memory. Tim Hanseroth posted an IG video of himself running through their studio albums and strumming along to stir the old juices. Carlile said in a video livestream for fans on the tour’s eve that she would have a monitor for lyrics if she needed it. But at the show I caught, I barely noticed Carlile looking down at it… which I can’t say for most big tours I attend where the show is locked in for months straight. All of this risks making the tour seem like a stunt, which it kind of is. But the bigger reason for why it’s such a rousing success — and a reason why fans may remember these shows almost as well as Carlile and company remember their songs — is how many deeply moving moments are stirred up up in the shows, in the quietest bits that come between the outbreaks of hysterical shouting and sign-waving. Leaving the setlists up to fans, chance or God results in obscure picks and ironic juxtapositions that sometimes aren’t anything more than fun or curious, but are sometimes unexpectedly touching in a way that one of Carlile’s perfectly laid-out arena shows probably couldn’t be. Not just a mere test of skills, these concerts are really a nightly emotional chemistry experiment. On the right night — and the show I saw in Oakland was the right night — it might be transcendent, in a way that’s a little different even from the transcendent gigs we’ve seen before. Carlile had some notes before the show began; rather than restrictions, felt like promissory instructions about how to best proceed through a candy store about to open. “I can see your signs all the way back, and I will call on people all the way in the back,” Carlile declared at the top of the concert Nov. 7 at the Fox Oakland, the second on their tour. (She later made good on that, picking more people from the rear balcony than any other part of the audience, though the front rows did OK too.).”Everything is pretty much fair game,” she instructed — “any song that we’ve ever done.” She noted that they wouldn’t be open to attempting songs they’d never performed even once before, “so we’re not gonna be able to ‘Free Bird’ or ‘Sweet Home Alabama’ this shit. But we might be able to get away with the handful of covers we’ve done in the past. And listen,” she added reassuringly, “you don’t have to worry about me — I’m 45, so if there’s a song I don’t want to do, I will just say no.” But Carlile also wanted it understood that this was not meant to be a tricky pop quiz. “Don’t feel like this should be a ‘stump the band’-type deal,” she said. “We really want this to be musically awesome for you guys. We want you to love what you’re hearing and request the songs that you really want to hear. I’m a deep cuts girl. I love track 7 on everyone’s album. I’m a last track gal. And I know that you know that you’re never gonna hear those songs on the big tours that we do.” That said, she opened it up to the idea that predictability isn’t always a negative. “If you want to hear the fucking ‘Story,'” Carlile declared, “just request ‘The Story’!” Related Stories Apple Services Revenue Hits New Record of $31.6 Billion in September Quarter, but Growth Is Slowing Down No one chosen in Oakland wanted to choose the fucking “Story,” or “The Joke” or anything else that might qualify as too big a hit, possibly in fear of eliciting groans from a rarities-inclined audience. (It does feel safe to call her biggest songs hits, even if toward the end, listening to the roars for obscurities, she said, “It almost makes up for the fact that we never had a hit. If you’ve never had a hit, all your songs get to be hits with your buddies. I don’t think we need one.”) But Carlile stating her openness to doing more predictable songs did create a safety net for the audience, establishing that there would be no wrong answers or incorrect pleas. Also no duds, although one song choice did pose an unsolved mystery, with its unexpected popularity, which was resolved with a bit of discussion between performers and audience. A couple in the front row of the Fox Oakland’s balcony requested “Heart’s Content,” which got only light applayse Carlile then noted had also been requested the previous night in Portland… to her puzzlement. “I think this song’s gonna be requested every night,” she laughed, “because we never play it and it’s to me the most obscure song. Is it even on one of our albums?” It is — from 14 years ago — but it’s understandable why it’s never been a concert favorite: Perfectly pleasant-sounding, it’s the rare tune in her 21-year catalog that just doesn’t really sound like a Brandi Carlile. Phil Hanseroth relayed reportage from someone in the front rows: “It’s in a movie.” “What’s the movie?” “Safe Haven.” “Is it a romcom?” inquired Carlile. “Is it sad, like ‘The Notebook?’ Well, thank you — now I understand… A bunch of romcom fans up in here.” No judgments. There was a greater sense of consensus, on-stage and off-, about most of the rest of the 22 songs played in Oakland. The first chosen was “Raising Hell,” a rowdy oldie that made it clear that, among other things, Carlile and the twins have always harbored stomp-and-holler tendencies… with literal stomping, on a few occasions in this set, to add percussion into the mix. In the most extreme pendulum swing possible, next up among the requests was a song about raising heaven, “The Mother,” a gorgeously happy song that deals with motherhood very generally and gay motherhood very specifically. Carlile preceded “The Mother” with an extended anecdote about chaperoning the social life of her eldest daughter, who’s repeatedly named in the chorus — with a side note that the story should not leave the room, since Evangeline is at the age where it’s not easy to always discern whether she resents being talked about on stage or takes pride in it in any given moment. That alone, in the singer’s mind, justified the decision to have phones put away in Yondr pouches, something Carlile has not required at any of her previous gigs but wanted for these, both to create greater intimacy and to keep flubs from going up on YouTube. (There weren’t any blatant ones, although the Hanseroths did shoot knowing smiles at each other a couple of times when a note sounded a little bit interesting.) Carlile has often spoken before “The Mother” in concert, but the loose formatting of this show seemed to allow her to stretch out even more, over a period of minutes. “I remember having a really difficult time with it because Catherine carried both girls… Somebody talked me through it and told me I needed to come up with a mantra. And my mantra became, I have to tell myself I’m a mother so that I can believe I deserve to call myself that. So it became ‘I am the mother of Evangeline.’ And when I first wrote this song, I thought, ‘Well, this thing’s niche! You have to be a gay mom that didn’t carry a child to understand this song.’ And it’s not true — it’s a universal thing — because here I am in Oakland, and this man stood up and wanted me to play the song.” The mood swings got wilder from there, as “Folsom Prison Blues” was requested next, a cover Carlile figured they hadn’t done in a decade. (Actually, only seven years.) The twins spent a bit of time remember and working out the licks before a formal kickoff that led to some wildly exuberant death in Reno. From there, in another big turnabout, it was “Dying Day,” which they opted to do at the lip of the stage, without amplification, as they’d done in the distant past, albeit probably in slightly smaller rooms than the 2,800-capacity Fox. Voices carried. The tour offers an opportunity to witness problem-solving in real time. For Carlile and the twins, perhaps the biggest problem was obliging a request for Alanis Morissette’s “Uninvited.” This was not because of recent unfamiliarity with the tune — they performed it nearly every night on this year’s “Human” arena tour, among the encores — but because they’d never done it as an acoustic trio. Without the heightened drama of a string section and the number’s signature piano notes. “I have no idea how we’re gonna do this without strings. Love will find a way,” Carlile said. “And no piano? That’s the whole song!” But she and the brothers found their path to make it a pure guitar-and-bass rock ‘n’ roll scorcher, followed by an exultant “We don’t need no stinking strings!” (With implicit apologies, undoubtedly, to SistaStrings.) Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre “I Belong With You” was introduced as having been written “when I first met my wife, Catherine… I wasn’t a big love song girl. I didn’t really get them.” The monologue was interrupted when she went to greet a young girl in the front row who was having her own emotional moment. Hi babe. What’s goin’ on?… Don’t cry!” When she came back, she dropped the love-story intro, but did have some instructions for the Hanseroths: “You guys aren’t on in this one until four minutes.” They took five for four, and you didn’t have to look at your watch — but just for fun, I did — to know that she was right on target with her reminder to the bros, give or take 10 seconds. This was a woman who knows her own material, as was repeatedly evident when each request was immediately followed by a callout to her guitar tech about which instrument to bring out. (“That’s gonna be capo 8 for a strummer”… “‘That Year’ is gonna be Kalamazoo, capo 7.”) Carlile sang “Turpentine,” a song about physically battling with her brother growing up, with its wistful rejoinder, “I’m warning you, we’re growing up” — and though she didn’t directly make the connection this night, it was easy to surmise how growing up to close to her “Irish twin” brother prepared her for a life and career with the Hanseroth twins. She taled about writing “Stranger at My Door” in Australia, “jetlagged with a broken heart,” and bringing the new song to the twins in a club’s backstage alley. “‘Tell me the truth. Is it too much? Is it too many words?’ Phil’s like, ‘Eh, it’s a little wordy.’ Phil’s a 7 on the Enneogram. You know what that means?… You’re incredibly impatient, and this song is five minutes long and full of words and that’s why you guys love it!” she laughed, turning to the attending Bramily. Dolly Parton was saluted with “Jolene” — “She had a temper, she had a dirty mouth, and she had the biggest heart in the world,” said Carlile — and a call-out for some Joni Mitchell on that singer’s birthday went rewarded with an E-major “River.” The singer talked about a two-and-a-half-hour phone call while driving home on Halloween night, hearing even more wild stories from the legend than she’d already heard. “A lot of times she’ll end the story by going, ‘And that was where I found “Refuge of the Roads.”‘ Or, ‘And that’s why I shouldn’t have got on that plane.’ In those moments, I realized that, no matter what happens in my life, I got to listen to Joni Mitchell play solitaire and tell me her stories. She’s not lying. I’m not even sure she’s capable of it.” The last stretch of the Oakland concert lifted the show from delightful travelogue to a something heavier on some of the trio’s most emotionally incisive songs, although it was difficult to know whether they were making these selections intentionally or those requests were providentially just arriving right on time. Tim Hanseroth did say he’d been waiting all night to pick on the guy in the front rows holding a sign asking for “The Things I Regret,” and subsequently showed up on Instagram thanking the fan again. It raised one of those questions that can only arise at a rarities-filled show like this: Why was this not a bigger hit — even amongst the band itself? It’s got an unforgettable singalong hook and serious stomp-and-holler bona fides, and it’s about the accumulation of screw-ups that adds up to a lifetime’s worth. What more could you ask? Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre Jen Horton But the most touching highlights were “Most of All,” a song about seeing your family in yourself (there are few lines more evocative than “His heavy hands swing at the end of my arms”)… and “That Year,” an alternately chilling and warm ballad about looking to make peace with a high school friend who committed suicide, from across the veil that separates the living and the dead. And the recent “No One Knows Us,” about how each friendship bond formed among young people is precious, irreplaceable and worth the upkeep in a more depressed middle age. And the penultimate number, “That Wasn’t Me,” a neo-gospel ballad so healing and cathartic, it would have become Carlile’s signature song in some other lifetime, instead of a deep cut. The actual climax? A rare cover of Led Zeppelin’s “Going to California,” because Carlile can hit the golden-god notes. And then California surrendered the combo to the next stop in Tucson. (Where they did not get the Led out, of course, and where the next stop involved only repeating four of the 22 numbers heard in Oakland.) As a cherry on top, anyone leaving the show each night finds that there was a bonus offered earlier, not to them, but to anyone suffering at home with FOMO. Right before she takes the stage, when the local audience is already seated, Carlile does a livestream of a single song while she’s having her makeup applied, just for everyone who doesn’t have the privilege of the live show (though, of course, the concert crowd can catch up with it later). It’s a hell of a miniature grace note. Saying this was the best show I’ve ever seen by Carlile and company probably without saying, after saying all of that; at times, I got to thinking it was one of the best shows I’ve ever seen from anyone, out of untold thousands. Concert hyperbole is a dangerous thing, but I found myself hard-pressed to recall comparable instances in which I’d seen rock ‘n’ roll performers so throughly committed to the moment, not just for a moment but for close to three hours of them. Maybe that’s because I have a worse memory than Carlile and the Hanseroths, but more likely because this really is as good as it gets, if you have a taste for the rare intersection where hair-trigger meets tear-jerk. Adjust your settings for how many hundreds of dollars you’d pay for a resale ticket for the remaining dates accordingly. Courtesy of Everett Collection Spider-Man: Brand New Day and its stars Tom Holland and Zendaya, along with BTS, were among the big winners Saturday night at the Kids’ Choice Awards . Spider-Man: Brand New Day was named favorite movie, while Holland and Zendaya were named favorite movie actor and actress, respectively. title: Danny Boyle Talks ‘Ink’, The Common Architecture Of His Movies And More ‘28 Years Later’ As He Receives The Deadline Legend Award
full_text: Skip to main content By Patrick Hipes Patrick Hipes Executive Managing Editor More Stories By Patrick Danny Boyle Talks ‘Ink’, The Common Architecture Of His Movies And More ‘28 Years Later’ As He Receives The Deadline Legend Award Palm Springs Film Awards Honorees: Andrew Garfield Set For Spotlight Award, Actor MPTF Expanding Its Veterans Benefits Assistance Program Nationwide View All November 14, 2026 5:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Mike Fleming Jr. and Danny Boyle on Saturday at the DGA Theater Rich Polk/Deadline via Getty Images Danny Boyle says he used to believe that he that he never made the same film twice, thus a filmography that includes hit movies across genres like Shallow Grave, Trainspotting, 127 Hours, The Beach, 28 Days Later and of course Slumdog Millionaire , the 2009 Best Picture Oscar winner that also won him Best Director. But Boyle, speaking onstage Saturday after receiving the Deadline Legend Award during Deadline’s Contenders Film Los Angeles awards-season event, said he was set straight on that idea long ago. Related Stories News Danny Boyle Says Tabloid Headlines Censored In British Version Of ‘Ink’ Will Be Shown In U.S. News Deadline Studio At Contenders Film 2026: Mahershala Ali, Penélope Cruz, John Turturro, Tatiana Maslany, Peter Farrelly & More “I can’t remember if it was a press conference or a Q&A in Paris, and this French journalist stood up at the back and said, ‘This is nonsense, Mr. Boyle’,” he recalled. “And I said, ‘Excuse me, what?’ And she said, ‘All your films are exactly the same.’ She said, ‘They’re all about, and it’s usually a guy, who overcomes, who faces insurmountable odds and overcomes them.’ And with that she walked out.” He continued, “Ever since then I’ve accepted that she’s absolutely right — they are all about the same thing, really. And you do realize, and you can see in other filmmakers as well. You’re desperately trying to make a different film, and they basically turn out the same in a way. They’re the skeleton or the the kind of architecture of them is the same somehow. I have to hold my hand up and admit that. So if you keep buying tickets to go and see the films, thank you.” Watch on Deadline Boyle’s latest entry on his list is Ink , based on Hames Graham’s Tony-winning play about Rupert Murdoch and editor Larry Lamb’s efforts to revive the British newspaper The Sun , ushering in a new kind of tabloid journalism with lurid headlines and questionable tactics. Graham adapted the screenplay for the pic, which opened this year’s Venice Film Festival and is gearing for its December 11 release in theaters. In Ink ‘s case, the underdogs in question are Guy Pearce’s Murdoch and Jack O’Connell’s Lamb, who are faced with the daunting task to make inroads against a dozen UK paper including what Doyle called “the Real Madrid” of publications at the time, The Mirror . “One of them from Australia, and the other one from Yorkshire in the north of England, with a plan to beat [ The Mirror ] in a year, in just one year, to overtake it in a year,” Boyle said in conversation with Deadline’s Mike Fleming Jr. “And what they did in order to do that was, in my contention and James’, is that they invented the tabloid vernacular, the language, the the vocabulary, the techniques of the tabloid, and they began to use it. And it connected with what people in Britain wanted, who were still in a dreary world of paternalism and postwar ‘we know what’s best for you’ kind of mentality, and they suddenly found a kind of liberation.” That’s in the first half of the film, which he said “I hope is very very funny because it employs the tabloid techniques to to gain your trust really, but through your pleasure. Then it begins to change a little bit when you find out some of the things that they’re up to and some of the costs of what that approach entails.” Boyle during the conversation also confirmed that headlines that appeared in the movie’s epilogue that have been redacted in UK versions of the film because of stringent libel laws will be shown in the U.S. versions . He also said a difference from Graham’s play is Claire Foy’s character Jules Davies, a composite of several women who worked at The Sun including one that had an affair with Lamb. Lamb’s son objected to the inclusion, Boyle said, because he thought it disparaged the memory of his mother, “which is absolutely right,” the director says. “The film’s about Larry Lamb and his reputation and his behavior. And he was a public figure. And it’s only right and proper that we have the right to investigate him,” Boyle said. “He changed British society significantly in many ways, as much as Margaret Thatcher changed British society.” Thatcher also appears in the film. “We didn’t want an impersonator to play her, so we actually re-created her, the real Margaret Thatcher. But we didn’t ask Margaret Thatcher’s estate because these powerful people, we have to be able to investigate them, and provided you do it truthfully and responsibly …. I think it’s right to have that kind of artistic license. In fact, it’s crucial to freedom and artistic freedom that you do have that license with public figures. Boyle also provided an update on a third installment of the 28 Years Later franchise , after he and Alex Garland brought back the franchise in 2025. A second movie, Nia DaCosta’s 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple also penned by Garland, hit theaters this past January. “Alex has written a fantastic script. Seriously, he’s written a fantastic script, so we’ve got to raise the money to make it,” Boyle said. He also confirmed that Cillian Murphy , who appeared in the 2002 Boyle-directed franchise starter 28 Days Later , was game to return. “I mean, he’s up for it, and it’s a fantastic part — Alex has written this fantastic part for him,” Boyle said. “Those of you who saw [ Bone Temple ], he’s teased at the end of that, and then the third film does complete the story in a beautiful, mathematically perfect way in which the circle is closed in a way that even Chris Nolan might admire, actually, because it’s perfect. So let’s hope it all comes together.” Check back Monday for the video of the conversation. title: Richard Sterban, Oak Ridge Boys’ Bass Singer, Dies at 83
full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All November 14, 2026 4:39pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Richard Sterban Jason Kempin/Getty Images Richard Sterban, the Oak Ridge Boys’ bass singer who memorably lent his vocals to their beloved “Elvira” cover, died Saturday. He was 83. Sterban died in Hendersonville, Tennessee, due to complications from bronchitis and pneumonia after fighting a battle with cancer, his family and the Oak Ridge Boys announced. “We appreciate all of your love, support, and prayers. Please continue to lift us up in this difficult time, we find comfort knowing that he is currently face to face with Jesus,” Sterban’s family said in a statement. Related Stories Music Meet Plave, the Very Real Virtual K-pop Boy Group TV Skip Hinnant, Actor on 'The Electric Company' and Voice of Fritz the Cat, Dies at 86 Born on April 24, 1943, in Camden, New Jersey, Sterban began singing at 6 in Sunday school as a soprano. He sang tenor in his seventh-grade glee club, and upon his eighth grade, his voice dropped to bass. He studied music at Trenton State College (modernly known as the College of New Jersey), and began singing in a gospel quartet where he met Joe Bonsall, his future Oak Ridge Boys bandmate. While singing part-time, Sterban joined J.D. Sumner and the Stamps, whom Elvis Presley hired to sing behind him. He then sang and recorded with the King of Rock and Roll, and also appeared in the 1972 concert film Elvis on Tour . Sterban was then offered the opportunity to join the Oak Ridge Boys after the departure of Noel Fox, which he accepted in 1972. Bonsall joined the group one year later, with Duane Allen, William Lee Golden and Sterban already in the group, which carried on as the faces of the band for five decades. They performed with Johnny Cash , who helped them sign with Columbia Records in 1973, though it was after opening for Roy Clark in 1975 when they met his manger, Jim Halsey, who would later sign with the group. They reached success with “Y’all Come Back Saloon,” which reached No. 3 on the country chart in 1977, and led to a string of hits. “I’ll Be True to You” became their first No. 1 song, though 1981’s “Elvira” would become one of their largest successes. Originally recorded by Dallas Frazier, the Oak Ridge Boys’ version of the track went to No. 1 on the country chart and No. 5 on the pop chart, sold more than two million copies and won a Grammy. Sterban’s bass refrain was a major touchpoint on the song. The Oak Ridge Boys went on to also become members of the Grand Ole Opry, the Gospel Music Hall of Fame and the Country Music Hall of Fame. Sterban released his memoir From Elvis to Elvira: My Life on Stage , written with Steven Robinson, in 2012. Sterban is survived by his wife, Donna; his daughters, Lauren (Tyler) and Tori (Michael); his sons, Rich (Chele), Doug and Chris; his grandchildren, Mali (Zachary), Nikolas, Tyler (Ryann), Madelyn, Alexandra, Rex, Owen and Charli Grace; and his great-grandchildren, Salem, Asher and Theo. He was preceded in death by his mother, Victoria, brother, Joseph and grandson, Zachary. THR

title: Inside the Plane Where Simple Plan, Hoobastank and More Performed Mid-Flight as Planes Were Grounded Across the U.S.
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All November 14, 2026 3:26pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Hoobastank performs mid-flight. Anthony Hughes Have you ever been serenaded at 35,000 feet by Hoobastank ? We’re betting that answer is no. But about 125 lucky Southwest Airline passengers got that opportunity on Friday on a charted Southwest Airlines flight from Los Angeles to headed to the Vans Warped Tour in Orlando. The festivities actually kicked off that morning in Terminal 1 of LAX. At the gate, guests — who were mostly dressed in black, rock-themed attire, with plenty donning sort of Vans apparel, from shoes to purses to hats — were greeted with a rock music playlist as passengers had the opportunity to perform their favorites. (Shout-out to the woman named Gianna who gave a high-energy performance of Fall Out Boy’s “Sugar, We’re Goin Down.”) Then they were invited to a meet-and-greet with recording artists Lolo , Simple Plan , Hoobastank and The Used , all of whom are were on the Vans Warped Tour lineup. Related Stories Movies 'Fatherland' Wins Top Camerimage Prize as 'Wild Horse Nine' Nabs Audience Award TV Philomena Cunk Comes for Hollywood What some of the passengers — who included fans, influences and journalists — didn’t realize is that all four acts were going to perform on the flight to Orlando. The initiative is part of the airline’s Live at 35, an in-flight entertainment program — celebrating its 15th anniversary this year — that surprises passengers with live pop-up music performances and events at 35,000 feet. Once in the air, singer Lolo kicked things off somewhere over Texas with a four-song set. At one point, Lolo shared that she “almost didn’t take the gig because I’m a nervous flier and this is the longest I’ve gone without wearing a seat belt.” (Incidentally, the flight took off about an hour before the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all U.S. flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” The buzz on the plane was that our flight was likely one of very few planes in the air at the time.) The aforementioned Hoobastank performed a trio of sings, culminating with their 2004 smash hit “The Reason.” During that song, lead singer Doug Robb asked the flight staff to turn off all the lights and the passengers to turn on their cell flashlights, upping the concert vibe inside the aircraft. The passengers also took part in a rousing sing-along to the tune. “Is this the most annoying flight you’ve ever been on?” Robb joked. Walking through the plane, he swiped an iPad from a passenger who was evidently doing some online shopping. “I think you should buy that,” he joked. During his set, The Used frontman Bert McCracken noted the unusual “venue” as the flight was passing over New Orleans. “This is the weirdest fucking shit I’ve ever done in my life,” he quipped. The band played four songs, and also turned “The Taste of Ink” into a sing-along. (“Everyone knows the lyrics to this song. It’s called ‘The Reason,'” McCracken joked in a callback to Hoobastank’s crowd-participation performance.) Simple Plan’s Pierre Bouvier took the stage — floor? aisle? — last, performing songs including “I’d Do Anything.” After the song, he joked, “Give it up for Mark Hoppus,” the Blink-182 singer-bassist who is featured on the song. (Hoppus was not present.) Bouvier joked it was “super awkward” to perform on a plane, even changing the lyrics to “I’d do anything for you, Vans Warped Tour,” before giving a knowing look and quipping, “Really, anything .” Bouvier also sang “I’m Just a Kid,” noting that it went viral on social media several years after its release as part of the #ImJustAKidChallenge Challenge, where users re-created childhood photographs as adults or adolescents. As the plane began descending, Bouvier asked the flight crew to turn down the lights, quipping that “the flight crew didn’t know they were going to become the light crew.” Markus Lloyd is the host for these events, which have featured acts including Julian Marley (son of Bob), the Plain White T’s, Magic!, Shane Smith & The Saints, Barenaked Ladies, Imagine Dragons, Chris Young and Cassidy Pope. “What’s fun” about these experiences, he told THR, “is that when we’re heading someplace fun, like the Vans Warped Tour, or Vegas, the plane has already kind of turned up a bit. And so when you tell them they’re getting this extra thing, it’s like they won the lottery. They’re like, ‘Oh my gosh, I’m going to Vegas AND I get a concert in the place? And that’s when we go, ‘You can’t get this anywhere besides Southwest.'” For an encore on Friday’s flight, Hoobastank got up to perform one last song just moments before the flight landed safely in Orlando. THR
